source.version_note: Supplied author-formatted manuscript with a January2021 file timestamp, not the publisher layout. Crossref identifies the matching article in Cognition212:104666,July2021,DOI10.1016/j.cognition.2021.104666. Publisher version and external supplement not fully read.
source.verification_method: All36 supplied manuscript pages read; title/authors matched to Crossref. Figure1 visually inspected. Bibliographic corrections below are metadata-only and do not constitute reading the cited originals.

citation.title: Autonomous vehicles: How perspective-taking accessibility alters moral judgments and consumer purchasing behavior

reading.source_scope_note: Human hypothetical moral ratings, constrained budget allocation and stated buying/riding intentions under randomized scenario wording. The authors interpret two possible role categories as equal odds; quoted instructions do not specify a numerical lottery.
access_limits: All36 extracted pages read, including three experiments, all mediation tables, figures, general discussion and references. Figure1 on page12 visually inspected to check role and probability wording.

External supplemental scripts, raw data, PROCESS output, preregistration and final publisher full text were not opened or reproduced. Recruitment provider/country and complete exclusion details are not supplied in this manuscript.
Rawls, Harsanyi, Huang and cited perspective-taking originals remain unread. Crossref checks verify identity/locators only.

study.design: Three separate experiments, eachN300, sum900 reported participants; each2x2 between-subjects. Partial passenger-only description versus full possible-passenger-or-pedestrian description.
study.experiment_1a: N300,165female,mean age52. Other factor: oneself versus named strangerSam. Moral swerve-minus-stay rating and hypothetical £50,000 allocation difference.
study.experiment_1b: N300,152female,mean age48. Same design with anonymous stranger. Removes the name but retains same outcome and scenario format.
study.experiment_2: N300,160female,mean age51. Oneself versus oneself/family; one passenger/10pedestrians becomes2passengers/20pedestrians. Measures relative moral approval, willingness to buy and willingness to ride.
study.results: Full versus partial moral differences:1a5.00versus1.21;1b4.53versus1.14. Full increases reported utilitarian budget share. Experiment2 full/partial buy differences2.86/−1.09;ride2.90/−1.27.
study.causal_scope: Randomized wording bundles viewpoint access, role uncertainty, personal stakes and visual emphasis. Mediators and outcomes are all self-reports with randomized question order; mediator-to-outcome causation is not identified.
study.probabilities: Manuscript argues full access yields50/50 passenger/pedestrian odds. Its quoted stimulus says 'could be' in either role, and Figure1 says 'this could be you'; neither numerically states50%. Two possible categories do not alone imply equal probabilities.

summary: No new term is needed. Add direct empirical evidence for the existing perspective-taking accessibility entry and a second relevant own-safety preference source. Clarify that hypothetical allocation is not purchasing behavior, full role visibility is not demonstrated impartiality, and statistical mediation does not establish causal moral-to-purchase influence.

findings.definition: The availability of multiple relevant situational roles in a judgment task, here passenger and pedestrian rather than passenger alone.
findings.novelty_rationale: Already defined from the earlier critical review. This is the original experimental manuscript, a distinct fully read article, so enrich the existing entry rather than add an 'impartiality' duplicate.

evidence.quote: access to full or partial situational perspectives and
you could be one of the 10 pedestrians

findings.evidence_scope: ThreeN300 experiments randomly vary scenario wording and find higher swerve-minus-stay moral ratings, hypothetical utilitarian budget allocations or buy/ride intention differences under full role description. The version does not independently assign or measure a50/50 role lottery.
findings.boundary: This is a task condition, not a universal debiasing treatment. Viewpoint availability, actual perspective taking, role probabilities, self-interest and impartiality differ. Multiple role categories do not imply equal probabilities, and group-average consistency does not mean every participant is consistent.

findings.definition: Imagining oneself in another role or considering another person's situation, here operationalized through self/stranger and passenger/pedestrian instructions.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing broad construct. Imagine-self and imagine-other are variants within it, not automatically additional independent mechanisms.

evidence.quote: how one would feel in someone else’s situation
how someone else feels in their situation

findings.evidence_scope: The manuscript defines common perspective-taking variants secondarily and experimentally manipulates scenario accessibility. It does not directly measure successful mental uptake, empathy or all real-world stakeholder views.
findings.boundary: Providing a prompt is not proof that someone adopted an accurate perspective. The source's 'full' means the two selected task roles, not every affected person's interests, and no AI subjective viewpoint is established.

findings.definition: Favoring a policy that protects one's imagined own physical safety when choosing among harmful-outcome alternatives.
findings.novelty_rationale: The personal versus stranger contrast provides relevant evidence for the existing own-safety concept. It is not the same as attributional self-serving bias or proof that self-protection is unjustified.
findings.evidence_scope: Under partial passenger framing, personal involvement yields a negative utilitarian budget difference, while stranger involvement yields a positive one in1a/1b. Full role description produces positive means and an undetected self/stranger difference. These are hypothetical preferences, not actual willingness to incur mortal risk.
findings.boundary: The manipulation also changes personal relevance and anticipated consequences. A lower self-sacrifice preference can be defensible; the results do not isolate a unique egoistic process, prove elimination of self-interest or demonstrate real vehicle purchase.

findings.definition: Considering a choice while one's eventual role among those affected is unspecified; the authors present full accessibility as a proposed variant.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing reasoning method; the manuscript's critique of Huang and its own reinterpretation require boundaries rather than another VOI label.
findings.evidence_scope: The discussion contrasts equal person-level sampling in Huang with the authors' assumed equal role categories. The experiment does not specify a numerical lottery in the quoted instructions or test Huang's original procedure independently.
findings.boundary: Equal roles are not equal chances for every person when group sizes differ. Higher survival probability for the same binary outcomes is first-order dominance, not sufficient evidence of risk aversion. The source's 'no self-interest or bias' conclusion is not established.

methodological_limits: The treatment bundles expanded perspective information with changing a known personal role into an unspecified role and altering expected personal stakes. The randomized effect is of that bundled description, not a uniquely identified accessibility mechanism.

The quoted full-access instructions and Figure1 name two possible roles but provide no explicit numerical probability. The50/50 interpretation is an author assumption; no reported comprehension or probability-perception measure confirms it.

Even a genuine50/50 passenger-versus-pedestrian category lottery differs from equal probability over all11 people. Equality of category labels does not establish impartiality, democratic legitimacy or a morally correct weighting.

If the two action options have the same50% personal survival probability, that can remove one expected personal-benefit difference, but uncertainty and self-interest remain. The source's claim that bias and risk-related preferences are thereby absent is not tested.

The manuscript calls9/10 survival 'risk averse' and1/10 survival 'risk seeking'. With identical binary outcomes, preferring greater survival probability is first-order stochastic dominance and is compatible with many risk attitudes; it does not diagnose risk aversion.

The £50,000 must be fully allocated between two cars; there is no outside option, actual payment, purchase or opportunity cost. The difference score measures relative allocation, not a real market price premium. The authors themselves later acknowledge allocation does not establish a desire to buy.

Experiment2 adds stated buying/riding intentions but no behavioral follow-up. Positive swerve-minus-stay differences can coexist with low willingness toward both vehicles. No actual adoption delay or reduction in casualties is measured.

All moral/purchase outcomes are transformed to swerve-minus-stay differences. Similar signs of group means do not establish equality across response scales, within-person consistency or elimination of every participant's judgment–action gap.

PROCESS bootstrapped indirect associations are not proof that moral judgment caused allocation or intention. Mediator/outcome order is randomized, not fixed temporally, and common-method or reverse-causation explanations remain.

Negative standardized mediation coefficients reflect predictor direction/coding, not evidence that full accessibility lowers utilitarian preferences. Do not 'correct' their signs solely because group means rise under full access.

The full-condition self/stranger and family comparisons withF<1 are null tests, not equivalence or proof of eliminated differences. Reported interactions support some moderation but cannot establish exact equality.

In Experiment2, family involvement also doubles both passenger and pedestrian counts, holding a ratio but changing group sizes. Any family effect is confounded with absolute numbers and possible different relational framing.

Retrospective power is reported for a conventionally large effectf.40. That does not establish precision for small interactions, mediation mechanisms or a null-equivalence claim. The manuscript does not provide a preregistered effect-based stopping rule beyond a14-day collection description for1a.

Recruitment is through an unnamed online service, with £1 compensation and little exclusion/attrition detail. Country, comprehension, overlap across cohorts and generalization need the external materials before stronger claims.

The manuscript uses 'prosocial' and 'utilitarian' evaluatively. Saving a greater number in a forced scenario does not establish that every rights concern, passenger-protective choice or alternative legal policy is irrational or antisocial.

Presented full information includes only passenger/pedestrian roles and known binary fatal outcomes. Real traffic has other parties, uncertain injury, prevention and legal duties. Balanced information should inform consent, not be used to steer adoption by hiding tradeoffs.
Publisher metadata identify the matching article, but the supplied36-page author manuscript may differ from the final version. Critiques are scoped to what was actually read.

cross_paper_learning.finding: The previously read critical review summarized this approach. The original supplied manuscript confirms role-access effects but its quoted instructions/Figure1 do not explicitly assign50/50 odds. Record the distinction between author interpretation and an experimentally stated lottery.

Known assigned roles affect own-safety choices; here roles become possible alternatives. Those manipulations differ, so neither demonstrates that perspective taking always removes self-protection or uniquely identifies impartiality.

Equal survival chances in a stated collision lottery are not the same as assumed equal probabilities of occupying categories. Neither design can be translated into real purchase or a universally justified AV policy.

Context-sensitive moral judgments can be observed without proving which internal reasoning process generated them. Bootstrapped mediation, like a preference graph, does not settle a unique psychological cause.

deferred.reason: Variants of the existing perspective-taking construct; source-specific roles are not independently established new behaviors.

deferred.term: Internal preference consistency as a new bias
deferred.reason: A descriptive relation between ratings and choices, not inherently a cognitive defect. Group means and difference scores do not define a distinct causal mechanism.

deferred.term: Risk aversion from choosing higher survival probability
deferred.reason: The stated contrast is compatible with dominance and does not identify curvature of utility or preference under matched expected outcomes.

deferred.term: Guaranteed impartiality or elimination of all self-interest
deferred.reason: Two viewpoints or equal category odds do not establish these conclusions. No direct measure or adequate falsification of those mechanisms is supplied.

deferred.term: Proven marketing intervention for actual adoption
deferred.reason: Hypothetical allocation and stated willingness are not actual purchase, policy acceptance or traffic safety outcomes.

limitations: No duplicate entry is added. Existing concepts gain source-specific evidence and explicit primary-manuscript boundaries. Cited books remain unread; no ethical edge, real-adoption effect, fabricated paper quota or annual series is added.
